country.comment: Study examines independent water systems in the municipality of Huajuapan de León, state of Oaxaca, Mexico.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title; PDF p. 2, Resumen; PDF p. 3, Abstract; PDF p. 21, Localización del área de estudio

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative multiple-case study with descriptive institutional and municipal statistics; no inferential statistical effect estimate reported.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across the 153 localities of Huajuapan de León, user-governed Independent Water Systems (SIAs) supply 38 localities (23% of the population; 19,229 inhabitants), the municipal utility SAPAHUA supplies 88 localities (70%; 58,524 inhabitants), and 27 localities lack continuous water supply. Although unrecognized in Mexico's National Waters Law (LAN) and excluded from formal river-basin councils unless holding legal personality and concessions, the four studied SIAs sustain intermittent piped water supply (ranging from 2 hours every third day to 6–12 hours twice weekly, at $30–$75 MXN/month) with greater water quantity and quality than municipal supply from the contaminated Yosocuta dam. SIAs face three main tensions: (1) financial/operational strain because monthly tariff revenues ($7,300–$48,000 MXN) barely cover pumping electricity costs ($8,000–$35,000 MXN), worsened by non-paying users invoking the human right to water to prevent disconnection and by municipal delays in public works; (2) coverage limits on rapidly urbanizing communal/ejido peripheries with clandestine private land subdivisions, where SAPAHUA steps in and blurs service boundaries; and (3) resistance against municipal pressure to take over SIA wells and infrastructure.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative multiple-case study (capped at 2 by design ceiling) that directly documents how statutory non-recognition under the LAN, community committee rules, tariff/electricity cost constraints, human-right-to-water non-disconnection claims, peri-urban agrarian/private tenure shifts, municipal public-works delays, and municipal takeover pressures shape water access, coverage, continuity, and quality.
